results.name: repdigit_target_rate_in_repdigit_sets
results.description: In sets containing at least one repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate on non-example repdigit targets; observed > null means people hold a "same-digit numbers" concept the model lacks (it under-produces repdigit generalisation); observed < null that it over-credits them.
results.code:
# name: repdigit_target_rate_in_repdigit_sets
# description: In sets containing at least one repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate on non-example repdigit targets; observed > null means people hold a "same-digit numbers" concept the model lacks (it under-produces repdigit generalisation); observed < null that it over-credits them.
def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    Xi = np.nan_to_num(X).astype(int)
    rep_ex = (valid & (Xi % 11 == 0) & (Xi > 0) & (Xi < 100)).any(1)
    rep_t = (t % 11 == 0) & (t < 100)
    is_ex = (valid & (Xi == t[:, None])).any(1)
    m = rep_ex & rep_t & ~is_ex
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: target_popularity_dispersion
results.description: Standard deviation across target numbers (pooled over all sets, targets with >=27 responses) of each target's overall yes-rate; observed > null means some numbers are intrinsically favoured/disfavoured as targets (a set-independent target prior) beyond what the model's set-target features predict; observed < null means the model over-differentiates targets.

results.name: divisor_target_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on targets (>=2) that are proper divisors of some example, excluding examples and targets sharing any example's final digit; observed > null means people generalise "downward" to factors of the examples (e.g. 16 -> 8, 100 -> 25) more than the model, which only credits multiples/counting up; observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: divisor_target_yes_rate
# description: Yes-rate on targets (>=2) that are proper divisors of some example, excluding examples and targets sharing any example's final digit; observed > null means people generalise "downward" to factors of the examples (e.g. 16 -> 8, 100 -> 25) more than the model, which only credits multiples/counting up; observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None].astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    Xf = np.where(valid, X, 1e9)
    is_div = valid & (t >= 2) & (t < Xf) & (np.mod(Xf, t) == 0)
    same_digit = valid & (np.mod(Xf, 10) == np.mod(t, 10))
    is_ex = valid & (Xf == t)
    m = is_div.any(1) & ~same_digit.any(1) & ~is_ex.any(1)
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())

results.name: digit_rule_violation_parity_gap
results.description: Among sets whose examples all share one final digit, yes-rate on digit-breaking targets of the same parity as the examples minus on those of opposite parity; observed > null means people still credit parity under an explicit digit rule more than the model's rule-pre-empted parity credit allows; observed < null means parity matters even less than the model assumes once a digit rule is evident.
results.code:
# name: digit_rule_violation_parity_gap
# description: Among sets whose examples all share one final digit, yes-rate on digit-breaking targets of the same parity as the examples minus on those of opposite parity; observed > null means people still credit parity under an explicit digit rule more than the model's rule-pre-empted parity credit allows; observed < null means parity matters even less than the model assumes once a digit rule is evident.
def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    n = valid.sum(1)
    d = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(X), 10), np.nan)
    dmin = np.nanmin(d, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(d, axis=1)
    viol = (n >= 2) & (dmin == dmax) & ((t % 10) != dmin)
    same_par = (t % 2) == np.mod(dmin, 2)
    a = viol & same_par; b = viol & ~same_par
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: size_principle_four_vs_three
results.description: Among sets whose examples all share one final digit, yes-rate on targets breaking that digit for 4-example sets minus for 3-example sets; observed > null means the model's linear per-example size penalty over-rejects at 4 examples (human rule confidence saturates by 3); observed < null means people's rejection keeps growing faster than the model's linear penalty.
results.code:
# name: size_principle_four_vs_three
# description: Among sets whose examples all share one final digit, yes-rate on targets breaking that digit for 4-example sets minus for 3-example sets; observed > null means the model's linear per-example size penalty over-rejects at 4 examples (human rule confidence saturates by 3); observed < null means people's rejection keeps growing faster than the model's linear penalty.
def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    n = valid.sum(1)
    d = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(X), 10), np.nan)
    dmin = np.nanmin(d, axis=1); dmax = np.nanmax(d, axis=1)
    uniform = (n >= 2) & (dmin == dmax)
    viol = uniform & ((t % 10) != dmin)
    a = viol & (n == 4); b = viol & (n == 3)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: numeric_interval_interpolation
results.description: In multi-example sets with no shared-digit rule and no common factor >=2, among targets sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets strictly inside the examples' numeric range [min,max] minus those outside it; observed > null means people use the fine-grained numeric interval spanned by the examples more than the model's decade-band familiarity captures; observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: numeric_interval_interpolation
# description: In multi-example sets with no shared-digit rule and no common factor >=2, among targets sharing no example's final digit, yes-rate for targets strictly inside the examples' numeric range [min,max] minus those outside it; observed > null means people use the fine-grained numeric interval spanned by the examples more than the model's decade-band familiarity captures; observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    n = valid.sum(1)
    Xi = np.nan_to_num(X).astype(int)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(Xi, axis=1)
    d = np.where(valid, Xi % 10, -1)
    dmin = np.where(valid, d, 99).min(1); dmax = np.where(valid, d, -99).max(1)
    same_digit = (valid & (d == (t % 10)[:, None])).any(1)
    lo = np.where(valid, X, np.inf).min(1); hi = np.where(valid, X, -np.inf).max(1)
    base = (n >= 2) & (dmin != dmax) & (g < 2) & ~same_digit
    inside = (t > lo) & (t < hi)
    a = base & inside; b = base & ~inside
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: single_digit_match_gain_four_sets
results.description: In 4-example sets whose examples do NOT all share a final digit, yes-rate on non-example targets sharing the final digit of exactly one example minus on targets sharing none; observed > null means a single matching exemplar boosts acceptance more than the model's averaged (1/4-weighted) similarity allows (max-like rather than mean-like exemplar matching); observed < null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: single_digit_match_gain_four_sets
# description: In 4-example sets whose examples do NOT all share a final digit, yes-rate on non-example targets sharing the final digit of exactly one example minus on targets sharing none; observed > null means a single matching exemplar boosts acceptance more than the model's averaged (1/4-weighted) similarity allows (max-like rather than mean-like exemplar matching); observed < null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()[:, None].astype(float)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    n = valid.sum(1)
    d = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(X), 10), -1)
    dmin = np.where(valid, d, 99).min(1); dmax = np.where(valid, d, -99).max(1)
    uniform = dmin == dmax
    cnt = (valid & (d == np.mod(t, 10))).sum(1)
    is_ex = (valid & (X == t)).any(1)
    base = (n == 4) & ~uniform & ~is_ex
    a = base & (cnt == 1); b = base & (cnt == 0)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: factor_rule_nonmultiple_rejection
results.description: In multi-example sets whose common factor g is >=3 and not a multiple of 5 (the model's common-factor rule), yes-rate on targets that are NOT multiples of g and share no example's final digit; observed < null means people reject rule-violating targets more firmly than the model (which only lacks a boost for them); observed > null means the model over-rejects them.
results.code:
# name: factor_rule_nonmultiple_rejection
# description: In multi-example sets whose common factor g is >=3 and not a multiple of 5 (the model's common-factor rule), yes-rate on targets that are NOT multiples of g and share no example's final digit; observed < null means people reject rule-violating targets more firmly than the model (which only lacks a boost for them); observed > null means the model over-rejects them.
def test_statistic(df):
    X = df["number_set"].str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy(float)
    valid = ~np.isnan(X)
    Xi = np.nan_to_num(X).astype(int)
    g = np.gcd.reduce(Xi, axis=1)
    n = valid.sum(1)
    same_digit = (valid & (Xi % 10 == (t % 10)[:, None])).any(1)
    m = (n >= 2) & (g >= 3) & (g % 5 != 0) & (t % np.maximum(g, 1) != 0) & ~same_digit
    if m.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m].mean())
